title: 8,000 steps on one or two days a week: what ten years of death records show [threshold, ard_1_2]
teaser: Among 3,101 US adults, reaching 8,000 steps on only 1 to 2 days a week was associated with a 10-year risk of death 14.9 points lower than never reaching it. [sample, threshold, ard_1_2, followup] The comparison is less clean than it sounds. [-]
hook: Step counts are usually sold as a daily target. [-] This study asked a different question: does it matter on how many days of the week you get there? [threshold]
populationPanel: Who was studied: 3,101 US adults aged 20 or older who wore an accelerometer for 1 week in 2005-2006 and were then traced through national death records. [sample, cohort] Nobody was assigned to walk more or less, so this is an observational study. [cohort] It describes these adults. It is not a prescription. [-]

card.headline: lower 10-year risk of death, compared with 0 days a week. [ard_1_2, followup, threshold]
card.support: People who reached 8,000 steps on 1 to 2 days a week, after the study's adjustments. [ard_1_2]

sections.heading: What they found
paragraphs: Researchers sorted people by how many days that week they reached 8,000 steps: none, 1 to 2 days, or 3 to 7 days. [threshold] Within 10 years, 40.7% of the people with no such days had died, against 14.1% of those with 1 to 2 days and 5.5% of those with 3 to 7. [followup, threshold, crude_0, crude_1_2, crude_3_7]

Those raw figures flatter walking, because the three groups were very different people. [-] After the researchers accounted for age, sex, smoking, existing illness and average daily steps, the 1-to-2-day group still had a 10-year risk of death 14.9 points lower than the zero-day group. [ard_1_2, followup, models] For 3 to 7 days the figure was 16.5 points. [ard_3_7] That is only a little more, and the curve went flat at 3 to 4 days. [plateau]

sections.heading: How sure is that number?
paragraphs: The 95% confidence interval for the 1-to-2-day group runs from 18.8 points down to 10.9 points. [ard_1_2] So even the weakest reading that fits the data is a 10.9-point gap, which is wide for a study of deaths. [ard_1_2] What the interval cannot tell you is whether the walking is the reason for the gap. [-]

sections.heading: What most summaries miss
paragraphs: The zero-day group had a mean age of 63.7. [ages] The 3-to-7-day group had a mean age of 46.0. [ages, threshold] Half of the zero-day group, 50.5%, said they had difficulty walking 0.25 miles or climbing 10 stairs, against 6.8% of the most active group. [mobility, mobility_def]
People who are already unwell walk less and die sooner, so part of the gap is illness, not walking. [confounding] The authors adjusted for this and say plainly that some of it remains. [confounding]
One more detail: the gap was 7.4 points in adults under 65 and 19.9 points in those 65 and over. [ard_1_2_under65, ard_1_2_65plus]

sections.heading: A related idea
paragraphs: The authors point to an earlier pooled analysis in which risk stopped falling at 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day for adults over 60, and at 8,000 to 10,000 for younger adults. [parallel_meta] Both findings describe the same shape from two directions: steep at the bottom, flat at the top. [parallel_meta, plateau]
Moving the daily threshold anywhere between 6,000 and 10,000 steps gave similar results, so 8,000 is a convenient marker, not a magic line. [thresholds, threshold]

limitations: Steps were measured for only 1 week, at the start. [one_week] How these people walked over the following 10 years is unknown. [one_week, followup]
This is an observational study. [cohort] People in poor health walk less and are more likely to die, and no adjustment removes that completely. [confounding]
Wearing a tracker can make people more active for that week, which would place some usually inactive people in the wrong group. [hawthorne]

figure.caption: The gap in deaths that went with days at 8,000 steps. [threshold, ard_1_2, ard_3_7] The study watched people and assigned nothing, so this figure has no arrow. [-]
figure.alt: Two bars and a bracket. [-] For people with 1 to 2 step days a week, the risk of death was 14.9 points lower. [threshold, ard_1_2] For people with 3 to 7 step days, it was 16.5 points lower. [threshold, ard_3_7] The bracket under both bars says they were seen together. [-]

takeaways: If a daily target keeps failing, the study's lowest active group is a reasonable place to start: 8,000 steps on 1 to 2 days a week. [threshold, ard_1_2]
Past 3 to 4 such days the association flattened, so a missed day is no reason to write off the week. [plateau]
The association was widest in adults aged 65 and over, at 19.9 points against 7.4 points in younger adults. [ard_1_2_65plus, ard_1_2_under65]
